title: Homeowners and renters translate inflation information into different spending responses
source_unit: NBER Working Paper 33595, revised July 2026; randomized inflation-information treatments among U.S. households with homeowner/renter comparison
geography: United States; household information experiment and homeowner/renter subgroups

observations.period: 2025 working paper, revised July 2026; randomized information-treatment results

denominator.unit: U.S. household experiment participants; exact analytic denominator is source-specific

renter_durable_spending.value: no detected adjustment in durable purchases

homeowner_expectation_update.value: more modest revision of inflation expectations

mechanism.value: attention and available adjustment margins differ by homeownership status; renters are more likely to be liquidity constrained

observations.method: Randomized information treatments on U.S. household inflation information, comparing belief updating and durable-spending responses by homeownership status; the study interprets the negative covariance between belief updating and spending response through attention and adjustment margins.
observations.uncertainty: The abstract does not disclose the full experiment denominator or all treatment details. Expectations and durable spending are not total welfare, household security, political attribution, trust, or voting. Homeownership is a resource and balance-sheet position, not a complete measure of liquidity or adjustment capacity.
observations.subgroup: Homeowners versus renters in the experiment; the contrast should not be generalized to all tenure, wealth, age, debt, or housing-market contexts.
observations.counterinterpretation: Homeowners may respond through housing wealth, credit, or durable-goods timing, while renters may adjust through nondurable spending, work, or delayed purchases not captured by the reported outcome. Different attention or trust in the information source may also contribute.

boundary: This record adds a controlled belief-to-spending and unequal-adjustment-margin mechanism. It does not establish a political action effect, total welfare, realized inflation exposure, or a complete household event-to-recovery path.
